Introduction

This report looks at how population size and growth relate to carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions across countries. It describes the population data, projects the 2030 population with the given exponential formula, shows how population and emissions have changed over time, and compares population counts with per-capita CO2 emissions.

Data preparation and exploratory analysis

The population file has 234 rows and 17 columns. The CO2 file has 215 rows and 35 columns before the duplicate 2019 column is removed. Population values are recorded at a few points in time (every ten years, or at selected years), while CO2 emissions are given for every year from 1990 to 2019. The CO2 measure is metric tons per capita, not a country total.

Outlier screening

The table below uses the 1.5-IQR rule for the main numeric variables. The boxplots use a log scale for population, area, and density where that makes them easier to read. Countries with extreme but real values (very large populations or very high densities) are kept. Being flagged by a boxplot does not mean the value is wrong.

outlier_long <- population |>
  select(country_name, pop_2022, area_km2, density, growth_factor, world_pct) |>
  pivot_longer(-country_name, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value")

  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.45) +

       title = "Distributions and flagged values") +
  theme_minimal()

Population projection to 2030

The Growth Rate column is a multiplier, so 1.01 means about 1% growth per year. The decimal rate is therefore \(r = \text{Growth Rate} - 1\). The projection uses t = 8 years in N[t] = P * exp(r * t), with the 2022 population as P. Keeping the rate constant until 2030 makes this an illustration rather than an official forecast.

top10 |>
  select(country_name, pop_2022, annual_growth_rate, pop_2030) |>
  mutate(across(c(pop_2022, pop_2030), round)) |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Country", "2022 population", "Annual rate", "Projected 2030"),
    caption   = "Projection for the ten most populous countries"
  )

Population trends

Ten most populous countries in 2022

ggplot(top10, aes(x = reorder(country_name, pop_2022), y = pop_2022)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2878B5") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Population",
       title = "Ten most populous countries in 2022") +
  theme_minimal()

Available population trend observations, 1990-2022

Population values are available for 1990, 2000, 2010, 2015, 2020, and 2022. The lines join these points, so they should not be read as yearly data.

ggplot(top10_trend, aes(x = year, y = population,
                        color = country_name, group = country_name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1990, 2000, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2022)) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Population", color = "Country",
       title = "Population of the 2022 top ten, 1990-2022") +
  theme_minimal()

CO2 emissions trend for the top ten

Country codes are used to match records that differ slightly in name (for example, different spellings or official names) before the join on standard names. The emission values are per capita. Missing country-year values are left as missing and skipped in the line plot.

ggplot(top10_co2, aes(x = year, y = co2_per_capita,
                      color = country_name, group = country_name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "CO2 emissions (metric tons per capita)",
       color = "Country",
       title = "Per-capita CO2 in the top ten countries, 1990-2019") +
  theme_minimal()

Correlation analysis

Population characteristics

The numbers below show how area, density, annual growth rate, and share of world population are related to each other. A correlation does not mean one variable causes another.

round(correlation_matrix, 3)
##                    area_km2 density annual_growth_rate world_pct
## area_km2              1.000  -0.063             -0.014     0.453
## density              -0.063   1.000             -0.070    -0.028
## annual_growth_rate   -0.014  -0.070              1.000    -0.021
## world_pct             0.453  -0.028             -0.021     1.000
ggplot(correlation_long, aes(variable_x, variable_y, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", correlation)), size = 4) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B",
    midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Correlation",
       title = "Correlation heatmap for population variables") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1))

2022 population and 2019 CO2 emissions

There are 191 countries with both a 2022 population and a 2019 emission value. Pearson’s correlation is 0.014 (0.843). Because population is heavily skewed, the regression uses log10 population. It describes the link with per-capita emissions, not with total emissions.

ggplot(merged_complete, aes(x = pop_2022, y = co2_2019)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65, color = "#2878B5") +
  geom_smooth(aes(x = pop_2022), method = "lm", se = TRUE,
              formula = y ~ log10(x), color = "#B2182B") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "2022 population (log scale)",
       y = "2019 CO2 emissions (metric tons per capita)",
       title = "Population size and per-capita CO2 emissions") +
  theme_minimal()

summary(population_co2_model)

Comparison by continent

The continent comparison adds up country-level 2019 per-capita values within each continent. This is an unweighted sum of per-capita figures and not a continent’s total CO2 emissions. To compare totals properly, a population-weighted figure or a total-emissions dataset would be needed.

kable(continent_totals, digits = 2,
      col.names = c("Continent", "Sum of country per-capita values"),
      caption   = "2019 per-capita CO2 sums by continent")
2019 per-capita CO2 sums by continent
Continent Sum of country per-capita values
Asia 290.55
Europe 246.67
North America 96.90
Africa 63.73
Oceania 54.78
South America 33.36 
ggplot(continent_totals,
       aes(x = reorder(continent, sum_country_per_capita),
           y = sum_country_per_capita)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3A923A") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL,
       y = "Sum of country per-capita values (metric tons per capita)",
       title = "2019 per-capita CO2 sums by continent") +
  theme_minimal()

In this sum, the highest continent is Asia (290.55). The third is North America (96.9), and the last is South America (33.36). These values should be read with the per-capita caveat above in mind.

Discussion, recommendations, and conclusion

Population grew noticeably in several of the most populous countries, but the exponential projection keeps each country’s 2022 growth rate fixed. Population size on its own does not tell us much about per-capita emissions, and the association found here should not be read as causal. The CO2 file also has missing values and reports emissions per capita, which limits what can be said about total emissions. Future work could use annual population data, describe a forecast model together with its uncertainty, and use total-emissions or population-weighted per-capita data for fair comparisons across continents.

This analysis covered data inspection, cleaning, visualisation, projection, country matching, and correlation and regression. The main point is that the meaning and units of a variable matter: adding per-capita values does not give a total.
